answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Frost, who reportedly said this around his eightieth birthday in 1954. Journalist Ray Josephs recorded the remark in a magazine profile, but no poem, letter, or manuscript in Frost's own hand confirms the exact wording — and no rival claimant has ever been identified for it.

source.excerpt: In three words I can sum up everything I've learned about life. It goes on.
trail: The line first appears in print in Ray Josephs's September 5, 1954 profile of Frost ↗, written around the poet's eightieth birthday.
Josephs's account was reprinted five years later in William Nichols's anthology Words to Live By ↗, which is the citation most quotation trackers now point to.

Quote Investigator's review of the paper trail concludes there is “substantive evidence” Frost said it, while cautioning that the exact wording depends on Josephs's testimony ↗ rather than a recording or manuscript.
source.excerptNote: This is not a line from a Frost poem or book — it is a spoken remark preserved only through a journalist's account, published about six months after Frost's eightieth birthday.

source.rightsHolder: Rights to the 1954 magazine account and its 1959 book reprint (Words to Live By, Simon & Schuster) rest with their respective publishers/estates, not with Frost's own estate.
source.rightsNote: The line was first fixed in print in 1954, inside Ray Josephs's copyrighted magazine profile and its 1959 anthology reprint, so it falls under standard U.S. copyright for post-1930 works rather than the public domain.

author.heading: About Robert Frost
author.metaLine: 1874–1963 · American poet, four-time Pulitzer Prize winner
author.bio: Robert Frost (1874–1963) was one of the most celebrated American poets of the twentieth century, four times awarded the Pulitzer Prize for collections including New Hampshire and A Further Range. His plainspoken verse on rural New England life carried a darker undercurrent of endurance and loss, themes shaped by a personal history marked by repeated family tragedy.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Robert Frost turned eighty in March 1954, and journalist Ray Josephs marked the occasion with a magazine profile built around a single line the poet reportedly offered when asked what life had taught him: “In three words I can sum up everything I've learned about life. It goes on.”

The remark resonated because Frost's own life had, quite literally, gone on through relentless loss — the deaths of his father, mother, and wife, plus four of his six children, alongside a sister and a daughter committed to psychiatric institutions. Read against that history, the line reads less like a greeting-card platitude and more like hard-won endurance.
detailsBody: The underlying sentiment predates Frost's tidy phrasing: poet Edna St. Vincent Millay had written “life goes on forever like the gnawing of a mouse” decades earlier, in her 1915 poem “Ashes of Life,” though her line is not a source for Frost's wording — the two are independent expressions of the same idea.
